title: The hook is not your video’s first sentence
markdown:
# The hook is not your video’s first sentence

At 7:42 p.m., a ceramics teacher props a phone against a mug, presses record, and says, "Hey everyone, today I want to show you a glazing trick." The trick is good. The bowl changes from chalky to deep blue in twenty seconds. Most people who see the opening will never find out.

The problem is not that the video lacks an introduction. It has one. That is often the problem. In a fast feed, an introduction makes the viewer wait while you arrange the furniture. The useful part is still in the hallway.

For a creator whose short videos keep getting swiped away, the fix is usually smaller than a new camera, a louder delivery, or another round of edits. Find the moment in the video that makes a particular viewer think, "Wait, I have that problem," and put that moment first.

## Start with the proof, not the greeting

The ceramics teacher has a much better first frame available: the finished blue bowl beside the dull one. Now the spoken line has somewhere to land: "This glaze looks gray until you make this one mistake." The viewer can see the claim before deciding whether to trust it.

That pattern works because the opening gives the eye and ear the same job. A spoken hook names a tension. The frame supplies proof, a result, or a question worth answering. If those two parts disagree, the video feels slow even when the words are sharp.

Try this with the footage you already have. Find the most revealing shot, the failed version, the odd before-and-after, or the precise result. Pull it to second zero. Then write the line that makes the shot matter. Do not explain the whole lesson. Give the viewer a reason to want the explanation.

## A topic is not yet a reason to stop

"I make videos about home workouts" is a topic. "If your knees hurt during lunges, your back foot may be doing too much" gives one person a reason to pause. The difference is not cleverness. The second line points at a moment someone can recognize in their own body.

Before recording, write this in plain language: "After this video, the viewer can ___ without ___." A food creator might write, "cook crisp tofu without buying a new pan." A freelance designer might write, "spot the sentence that makes a client brief unusable." The blank forces the video to promise a change, not merely announce a category.

If that sentence stays mushy, do not try to rescue it with suspense. The video may need a narrower point. "Three editing tips" can become "the cut to make before your tutorial starts." Smaller claims are often easier to believe and easier to film.

## Write different openings for the same video

Creators often spend an hour revising one hook when they need three genuinely different ones. Changing "stop" to "wait" is not a test. It is the same bet in a different shirt.

Take one finished idea and draft openings that make different promises. One can call out a familiar mistake. Another can show the result first. A third can challenge a piece of common advice. For the tofu video, those might be:

- "Your tofu is steaming because the pan is too crowded."
- "This is the crust you can get without a press."
- "You do not need to freeze tofu for a crisp edge."

Each line asks the viewer to stay for a different reason. The first speaks to frustration. The second puts a result on the table. The third earns attention only if the rest of the video can support it. That last part matters. A hook is a promise with a very short deadline. If the next beat wanders away from it, the viewer has been given a fair reason to leave.

Keep the spoken line short enough to say once without racing. Put only the essential words on screen. If you need a second sentence to explain what the first one means, the opening is still doing too much.

## Give the next second a job

Many hooks fail after they work. The first line creates a question, then the video cuts to a logo, a greeting, or a long explanation of why the creator made the video. That is where attention leaks out.

Plan the handoff before you film. After the opening claim, show the proof or first step immediately. After "Your tofu is steaming," show the crowded pan. After "This glaze looks gray," show the incorrect mix. The viewer should feel the video moving forward, not backing up to collect context.

A useful check is to watch the opening three seconds with the sound off. Can a stranger tell what is at stake from the image and on-screen text? Then cover the screen and listen. Does the line point to a real situation quickly? Finally, watch it normally. Does second four begin the payoff?

You will not turn every useful video into a hit by rewriting the first sentence. Feeds are crowded, and some subjects need more patience than short-form video allows. But a clear opening gives the work a chance. That is better than asking viewers to wait politely until it gets good.
